title: “WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS, THERE YOUR HEART WILL BE ALSO” — NOTICE WHICH ONE JESUS SAYS MOVES THE OTHER
paragraphs: “WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS, THERE YOUR HEART WILL BE ALSO” — NOTICE WHICH ONE JESUS SAYS MOVES THE OTHER

You may have spent years waiting for your heart to love God more before changing what you do with your money, time, attention, and possessions. But Jesus said something far more unsettling: sometimes you don’t wait for your heart to move. You move your treasure—and discover your heart has been following it all along.
There is a sentence from Jesus that many Christians can quote without realizing how dangerous it is to everything competing for their devotion.
We put it on wall art.
We underline it in our Bibles.
We hear it during sermons about money.
And because it sounds familiar, we can miss the blade hidden inside it.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” — Matthew 6:21
“Where your heart is, there your treasure will be.”
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
The Greek text preserves the force beautifully:
ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.
Hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Treasure. A store. Something laid up. Something considered valuable.
Not merely emotion in our modern sentimental sense, but the inner person—the center of desire, thought, intention, affection, and moral life.
But perhaps the most haunting word in the sentence is the ordinary-looking verb:
and then speaks of where the heart will be.
That does not mean every act of spending mechanically manufactures love, nor that Jesus is giving us a simplistic psychological equation.
Your treasure and your heart refuse to remain strangers.
What you continually prize, protect, pursue, accumulate, sacrifice for, invest in, and refuse to surrender becomes entangled with your inner life.
And Jesus does not merely tell His disciples to inspect their treasure.
He tells them to move it.
“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth... but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.”
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Maybe that explains something you have been unable to explain about yourself.
“Jesus, why don’t I desire You like I used to?”
And perhaps part of the answer is hiding in places we rarely examine during prayer.
The things you panic about losing.
The things you cannot imagine surrendering.
The things receiving the first and best of you.
Because treasure is bigger than money.
Money simply has an uncomfortable ability to expose treasure.
You can sing, “Jesus is everything to me,” on Sunday...
and then spend Monday through Saturday arranging an entire life around everything except Jesus.
You can say eternity matters most...
while almost every waking hour is invested in what expires.
You can say your children need Christ...
yet spend more energy preparing them to succeed financially than preparing them to stand faithfully before God.
You can pray for the lost...
and never inconvenience yourself for one.
You can say Scripture is precious...
while your phone receives hours and the Word receives leftovers.
You can tell Jesus, “You have my heart”...
while guarding your possessions as though they were your savior.
Not because He needs your wallet.
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Suddenly the question is no longer merely:
Because every treasure has a destination attached to it.
And your heart keeps learning the road.
This is why the surrounding words of Jesus matter so much.
Immediately after speaking about treasure and heart, Jesus speaks about the eye and whether the body is filled with light or darkness.
Notice what Jesus calls money in that sentence.
Produces resources that can carry the Gospel into places you may never personally enter.
But money becomes terrifying when the servant climbs onto the throne.
Because money does not have to ask you to renounce Christianity.
A little more and you will finally feel secure.
A little more and people will respect you.
A little more and you can stop worrying.
A little more and then you can become generous.
Until one day you possess many things—
and discover those things have been possessing you.
Jesus does not condemn responsible provision. Scripture does not teach that possessing material things is inherently sinful. Nor does Christianity teach that every believer must own nothing.
The danger is when the gift replaces the Giver.
When accumulation becomes the quiet answer to the question:
What do I really trust to keep me safe?
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings giving treasure to God.
It is the story of God giving His treasure for human beings.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son...” — John 3:16
Before you ever surrendered anything to Jesus...
He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death.
But through the precious blood of Christ.
The cross destroys every attempt to turn Christianity into a transaction.
You cannot donate enough money to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
“God has loved you in Christ—so what still owns you?”
The Gospel reaches into the clenched fist and says:
You can open your hand now.
Your possessions were never your savior.
Your bank balance cannot forgive you.
Your career cannot stand beside your grave and command you to rise.
Your reputation cannot wash away sin.
Your possessions cannot carry themselves through eternity.
Jesus can take the person who spent years chasing temporary treasure and rewrite the entire story.
Maybe your scandal is not the kind people gossip about.
Maybe your scandal is simply that you have called Jesus “Lord” while quietly allowing something else to function as lord.
Maybe the future you constructed in your imagination.
Anything can become the place where the heart begins building a home.
And sometimes the clearest evidence is not what makes you happy.
It is what you are terrified of losing.
Imagine Jesus sitting across from you tonight.
And what if He asked something even harder?
“If I am truly your treasure, what in your life proves that I am?”
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Jesus exposes idols because idols eventually devour the people worshiping them.
He does not point toward heavenly treasure because heaven needs your money.
He points toward heavenly treasure because your heart matters to Him.
Free from worshiping what rust can eat.
Free from being controlled by what thieves can steal.
Free from finding identity in what markets can erase.
Free from living terrified that tomorrow might remove what today gave you.
And notice what happens shortly afterward in Matthew 6.
“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness...”
These are not disconnected spiritual sayings.
What you treasure touches what you serve.
What you serve touches what you fear.
And Christ calls you away from slavery to temporary things and toward trust in the Father.
That is why generosity can become an act of spiritual warfare.
Not because every donation is automatically holy.
Not because giving money guarantees blessing.
Not because God can be manipulated by an offering.
But because sometimes opening your hand is how you tell an idol:
You are not my master anymore.
Sometimes giving to someone in need says:
Sometimes buying a Bible for another person says:
“The Word of God matters more than another unnecessary thing for me.”
“I want my earthly resources participating in eternal work.”
Sometimes quietly helping a struggling family says:
“My Father sees what nobody else needs to see.”
And sometimes generosity does something inside the giver that cannot be measured on a receipt.
your heart notices where it went.

This is why Paul told wealthy believers not to put their hope “on the uncertainty of riches, but on God,” and called them to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share, thereby storing treasure for the future.
There is a world of difference.
And Gospel Warrior must live under that same truth.
If this ministry ever asks you to support something while directing your heart away from Christ, do not follow that direction.
But if these articles have brought you back to Scripture...
if something you read here stopped you during a dark night...
if these words have helped you repent, pray again, forgive again, open your Bible again, or remember that Christ has not abandoned His people...
then consider whether you want to help keep that Gospel-centered work moving.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior proves you are a better Christian.
And not because you should ever give money needed for essential responsibilities merely because someone pressured you spiritually.
Support should come freely, prayerfully, honestly, and as an act of stewardship before God.
But glorifying God is not merely something Christians do with songs.
Scripture calls believers to glorify God with their whole lives.

So if you genuinely believe this ministry helps point people toward Jesus Christ, one practical way you can participate is by supporting it, sharing its biblical content, and helping put Christ-centered truth in front of another person who may desperately need it.
The discount is not the treasure.
The merchandise is not the treasure.
Gospel Warrior is not the treasure.
The purpose of everything should be to keep pointing beyond itself toward Him.
Jesus explicitly warned in this same chapter against practicing righteousness merely to be seen by people.
Somebody scrolling tonight may have everything money can buy and still feel completely empty.
Somebody may have walked away from church.
Somebody may be angry with God.
Somebody may be drowning in debt and shame.
Somebody may have made money their identity.
Somebody may be successful in public and spiritually starving in private.
Somebody may need one sentence to interrupt the direction of their life:
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Put that sentence in their path.
Because there may come a day when you need to read it again—not when you are poor, but when you are prospering.
Sometimes abundance tests the heart in ways suffering never could.
There is no shame in admitting that your heart has wandered.
The thief on the cross arrived at the end of his life with nothing to offer Christ except desperate faith.
Maybe grace is finding you in this paragraph.
Maybe you realize your treasure has been traveling in the wrong direction.
Then you do not need to pretend.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yesterday.
Turn your resources toward purposes that honor Christ.
And when you stumble tomorrow, return to Christ again.
Your salvation rests not in the perfection of your surrender but in the perfection of your Savior.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the Christian who is tired.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Invite the person who says they no longer believe.
Even invite the friend who might roll their eyes at you.
You never know which seed God may use.
Put biblical resources into people's hands.
Help someone move from endless scrolling toward Scripture.
Then become quiet enough to let the question hurt.
Look at what receives your first thoughts in the morning and your final thoughts at night.
And if you discover that your treasure has wandered...
The One speaking about treasure in Matthew 6 is the One who would eventually walk toward Jerusalem.
The Gospel is not God standing at a distance demanding treasure from sinners.
The Gospel is God coming near in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who treasured everything except Him.
We brought debt we could never repay.
He brought a cross and declared the work finished.
And now the risen Christ does not merely want a percentage of your possessions.
Not because your surrender purchases His grace...
but because His grace has purchased you.
So perhaps the question tonight is not:
“What has my treasure been teaching my heart to worship?”
Because someday everything you own will leave your hands.
Your hands entered this world empty.
One day they will leave it empty.
But if your treasure is Christ...
you will discover that death cannot steal your Treasure.
The grave could not hold Him.
And eternity will never exhaust Him.
So move your treasure toward what lasts.
Give when Christ calls you to give.
Share when truth deserves to travel.
Help people who cannot repay you.
Invest in Gospel work you have prayerfully judged faithful.
Because perhaps the most frightening tragedy would not be reaching the end of life and discovering you did not accumulate enough.
It would be discovering that you accumulated everything you wanted...
and trained your heart to live somewhere Christ was never your treasure.
Bring the hidden idol into the light.
There is still a cross for sinners.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still a Savior who receives repentant people.
And there is still time to change where you are laying up treasure.
A small public line marking a private surrender:
your heart will never remain far behind.
And maybe tonight, grace is asking you to move the treasure so your wandering heart can begin finding its way home.
When Christ becomes your Treasure, losing what cannot last no longer means losing everything.
